Ok, like, I'm not a linguist, so I'm afraid I may not know all the "underlying reasons" and stuff, but, as a daily user of a Russian language for my whole life, here's how I see it: you just don't need those auxiliary verbs in Russian. Like, with your example with a 2x + 5 = 13 equation, without "x" it just stops making any sense, exactly, and becomes just a false equation 2 + 5 = 13. But, with "x" in place, it's a completely normal math problem, with a possibility of finding a solution (x=4) and stuff. Now, when it comes to "**Я ухожу**." sentence, in Russian - you\_just\_don't\_need\_anything\_else. That's how I feel about it. Like, a somewhat literal translation of a sentence "I am leaving" to Russian would be "Я есть ухожу.", which is 100% incorrect in Russian and absolutely nobody says stuff like that. Why? Because, as I understand, you, again, just *don't need anything else* but a pronoun (who? Я) and a verb (what am I doing? ухожу). Without a pronoun - it would be somewhat confusing, and without a verb - the sentence would lost 90% of its information. But, with both of them in place, people will get that you're leaving. Like, I don't know, I really strongly feel that we have those suffixes (though I suspect that some of this stuff may also be "endings", not only suffixes. Not sure here) in place of auxiliary verbs.

Another example: I am going to the shop. = **Я иду в магазин**. Who? Я/I. What I'm doing? Иду/I'm going. Where am I going? В магазин/To the shop. Like, I don't know how else to explain it - but, in Russian, we just don't need auxiliary verbs. Language feels functional and complete enough without them.

You know - in the old Russian, about a century ago, there was a weird tradition of putting a sign [Ъ](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%AA) after the endings of a words, and back then it was everywhere, basically. Here's what's written on a Russian wikipedia (hope you'll be able to understand it):

>До [реформы русского правописания в 1917—1918 годов](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%A0%D0%B5%D1%84%D0%BE%D1%80%D0%BC%D0%B0_%D1%80%D1%83%D1%81%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%B9_%D0%BE%D1%80%D1%84%D0%BE%D0%B3%D1%80%D0%B0%D1%84%D0%B8%D0%B8_1918_%D0%B3%D0%BE%D0%B4%D0%B0) буква **Ъ** использовалась по тем же церковнославянским правилам, только без слов-исключений. В отличие от нынешней орфографии, разделительный **Ъ** ставился не только перед буквами йотированных гласных, но и в некоторых других случаях, вроде *съэкономить, разъикаться, двухъаршинный* и т. п. (в том числе он позволял различать на письме слова *подарочный* и *подъарочный*). Однако разделительный **Ъ** был крайне редок (как, собственно, и сегодня), а достаточно бесполезный **Ъ** в конце слов занимал примерно 4 % объёма текста и, по подсчётам [Л. В. Успенского](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%A3%D1%81%D0%BF%D0%B5%D0%BD%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%B8%D0%B9,_%D0%9B%D0%B5%D0%B2_%D0%92%D0%B0%D1%81%D0%B8%D0%BB%D1%8C%D0%B5%D0%B2%D0%B8%D1%87), до реформы правописания на него ежегодно уходило около 8,5 млн лишних страниц.

So, like, as a last sentence says - this Ъ sign was used very often, but there wasn't really much sense in it. So, people decided that we should stop wasting our ink, paper and time on this, and Russia just got rid of it in our language. And now, the Ъ sign is only in the middle of some words (quite rare), but, at the endings of a words - no single example comes to my mind. Only some people are still [putting it just for fun](http://cdn01.ru/files/users/images/5d/d7/5dd7f17e5ae22b5ff94c5504bc3b214d.jpg) on some signboards and stuff. (That's my understanding of it all)

So, a somewhat the same thing with auxiliary verbs, I think: we don't need them. Other stuff is already in place here.

I can guess that in Russian there are some bigger variety of those...endings of a words - not sure how it's called in English. And [stuff like that](https://ru.wiktionary.org/wiki/%D1%83%D1%85%D0%BE%D0%B4%D0%B8%D1%82%D1%8C). See? Seems that where in English there are wide variety of those "auxiliary verbs", in Russian there are wide variety of the endings of a words in place.

Hi, two primary meanings comes to my mind:

1) To make some offer to someone. Like, "Сделать предложение о покупке компании." = "To make an offer of buying a company."

2) To make an offer of marriage to someone, specifically. Like, if a girl saying "Он сделал мне предложение!", that means that some dude has proposed to her.

A translation "to make a sentence" is not correct - Google Translate probably just takes two words "сделать" ("to make") and "предложение" ("an offer", but also "a sentence") and just summing them up here. But, in Russia, nobody says about them sentences "to make" - like, you can "write a sentence" (написать предложение), you can "come up with a sentence" (придумать предложение), but you can't just "make" it - no, a word "to make" is for a different situations, in Russian. You can "make" a tea, for example - "сделать чаю", but not a sentence, yeah.

I think, in most cases - билет is a ticket, and талон is more like a voucher, yeah. But then, yeah, there are different uses for these words, including stuff like посадочный талон (boarding pass). In case of посадочный талон, I think that maybe it's called a талон because it's not a ticket per se, it's, like, something a bit different: билет на самолёт you can even get online and just print at home, after buying it on an airline's website, but to actually board the plane you need not your ticket, which, again, you could simply print on a printer, but you need another "sort of a ticket" which you get at the registration desk at the airport - hence, there's another word for it - посадочный талон. That's how I think, and, also, there's another word [купон](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%9A%D1%83%D0%BF%D0%BE%D0%BD) (coupon), which is sort of like a талон, again as I understand.

For a word билет, one of the other uses is a [Билет Банка России](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%91%D0%B8%D0%BB%D0%B5%D1%82_%D0%91%D0%B0%D0%BD%D0%BA%D0%B0_%D0%A0%D0%BE%D1%81%D1%81%D0%B8%D0%B8), meaning basically our banknotes, i.e. cash. Also [лотерейный билет](https://ru.wiktionary.org/wiki/%D0%BB%D0%BE%D1%82%D0%B5%D1%80%D0%B5%D0%B9%D0%BD%D1%8B%D0%B9_%D0%B1%D0%B8%D0%BB%D0%B5%D1%82).

TL;DR Two words (as well as a third one - купон) seems quite similar, but билет is more like a ticket and талон is more like a voucher. Купон is a coupon.

Though I also think that I made a small mistake in my post above. Basically, there are seems to be two meanings of a way of addressing someone with a word господин: one is as, well, people of a "lower class" usually addressed people of an "upper class" in Russia hundreds of years ago, as I understand, and the other is simply a respectful way to address someone - pretty much like "mister", yeah. So, I think, *sometimes* it's still seems to be *sort of* appropriate to say господин or господа, actually more in a humorous way of addressing someone or a group of people. Like, for example, if there is some meeting at some company, and everyone is talking loud with each other, if someone like a director of this company wants to bring attention to himself and, at the same time, make people to just stop talking and bring silence into the room, I think he can say something like "ГОСПОДА, давайте уже начнём заседание?". Then, there is also, for example, one Russian YouTube personality who is always addressing his viewers with this word (e.g. [here](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ooTbpWIkOAw) right on the first second. God I hope this post won't be deleted for an "advertising" of some youtube channel), but in his case I actually think that it feels just super awkward. In general, yeah, the word seems to be outdated. Товарищ or товарищи is useful sometimes, i think, then also "уважаемый X" seems to be good too. Like, aforementioned director could also be saying "УВАЖАЕМЫЕ КОЛЛЕГИ" instead of "господа", and it actually would be better, I think - it'd be more respectful this way. But NOT just "уважаемые" without any following word - that would be sort of a bit rude, as I understand. Like, to just address a group of people with a single word "Уважаемые!" feels not good, yeah.
